approachQuestion.prompt:
Turn the display strip. Reverse a mutable array cells of n fixed-size integer codes in place, so its original last code becomes first. Return no new array; the observable result is the changed input. There are 0 <= n <= 200,000 codes; repeats are allowed. You have permission to modify every cell, but must keep the same array allocation. Choose minimum worst-case time, then peak auxiliary storage. Indexed access, assignment, and swapping two codes have constant cost.

Example 1: Input: cells=[7,2,7,9]. Changed input: [9,7,2,7].
Example 2: Input: cells=[]. Changed input: [].

options.text: Use indices at the two ends, swap those codes, then move both indices inward until they meet or cross.
options.feedback: Each swap places two codes in their required final positions. The permitted mutation avoids any preservation copy.

options.text: Allocate a reversed copy of the array, then copy it back into the existing input allocation.
options.feedback: This respects the final allocation and produces the right reversal, but the full reversed copy is unnecessary when cells can be swapped in place.

options.text: For i from zero to n-1, assign cells[i] from cells[n-1-i] in the same array, without saving overwritten values.
options.feedback: For [1,2], the first assignment makes [2,2]; the next reads the overwritten value and cannot restore 1. It returns [2,2] instead of [2,1].

options.text: Sort the codes from largest to smallest within the array.
options.feedback: Reversal preserves the reverse of the original order rather than sorting by value. For [2,9,1], the required result is [1,9,2], not [9,2,1].

feedback.reason: Whether input may be changed determines whether preserving a full copy is necessary.
details: Initialize left=0 and right=n-1. While left<right, swap cells[left] with cells[right] using one temporary code, increment left, and decrement right. Return without allocating an output array.

Each swap fixes both outer positions permanently. An odd-length array leaves its middle code unchanged; an empty array performs no swaps. The original array allocation is the result, so mutation does not imply allocating a second array or a recursion stack.

“Use indices at the two ends, swap those codes, then move both indices inward until they meet or cross.”: Each swap places two codes in their required final positions. The permitted mutation avoids any preservation copy.

“Allocate a reversed copy of the array, then copy it back into the existing input allocation.”: This respects the final allocation and produces the right reversal, but the full reversed copy is unnecessary when cells can be swapped in place.

“For i from zero to n-1, assign cells[i] from cells[n-1-i] in the same array, without saving overwritten values.”: For [1,2], the first assignment makes [2,2]; the next reads the overwritten value and cannot restore 1. It returns [2,2] instead of [2,1].

“Sort the codes from largest to smallest within the array.”: Reversal preserves the reverse of the original order rather than sorting by value. For [2,9,1], the required result is [1,9,2], not [9,2,1].

complexityQuestion.prompt: For swap-inward, choose worst-case time and peak auxiliary space in terms of n, including the empty case. The mutable input is excluded, and no new array is output. The method is iterative; include its temporary swap variable.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard bound for the complete execution. Count peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage; exclude supplied input and required output.
Word arithmetic, indexing, and copying one fixed-size element take constant time. No hashing or recursion is used.

feedback.reason: At most floor(n/2) swaps use two indices and one temporary code.
details: There are floor(n/2) constant-cost swaps plus setup, so O(n+1) time, including an empty array. Two indices and one temporary code are constant auxiliary storage. The input remains the same allocation and no recursive stack, hash structure, or copied array is used.
“O(n + 1) time, O(n + 1) auxiliary space”: That extra memory belongs to a reversed-copy method, not the analyzed in-place swaps.
“O(n² + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Each step resolves two positions and no full traversal repeats inside a step; this upper bound is loose.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Swapping takes constant work per pair, but there are linearly many pairs as n grows.
